summary: A heap gives you the min (or max) in O(1) and lets you remove or insert in O(log N). Reach for it when you need the best element repeatedly, not once -- if you need it once, a linear scan is O(N) and simpler. The three heap shapes that cover almost everything: a greedy that always consumes the current smallest (connect ropes, job scheduling), a size-K heap of the opposite polarity for K-th largest/smallest, and two heaps facing each other for a running median. The greedy half of this chapter is the other side of the same coin: a heap is only the delivery mechanism, and the real work is proving that taking the locally best move is globally optimal. When the greedy order is fixed up front, a sort replaces the heap.

thoughtProcess.title: 1. Do I need the extreme repeatedly, or just once?
thoughtProcess.body: Once -> linear scan, O(N), done. Repeatedly, with inserts in between -> heap. That single question decides the whole problem. 'Find the min' is not a heap problem; 'keep taking the min while adding new values' is.

thoughtProcess.title: 2. K-th largest -> min-heap of size K (opposite polarity).
thoughtProcess.body: Counter-intuitive but fixed: for K-th LARGEST keep a MIN-heap capped at size K; the root is your answer. Push, then poll whenever size exceeds K. O(N log K) time, O(K) space. Flip both words for K-th smallest.

thoughtProcess.title: 3. Greedy that always consumes the current best -> heap.
thoughtProcess.body: If the optimal move is provably 'take the two smallest / the most profitable next', a heap is the data structure that serves that greedy in O(log N). Connect ropes, candy distribution, job selection. Prove the greedy first, then the heap is just plumbing.

thoughtProcess.title: 4. Running median -> two heaps, balanced.
thoughtProcess.body: Max-heap holds the lower half, min-heap the upper half. Keep their sizes within 1 of each other. Median is the larger heap's root, or the average of both roots when sizes are equal. Always push then rebalance -- never assume which side a value belongs to.

thoughtProcess.title: 5. Merging K sorted sequences -> min-heap of the K heads.
thoughtProcess.body: Push one node per list, poll the smallest, push that node's successor. O(N log K) instead of O(N log N) from concatenate-and-sort, and it streams -- you never hold all N at once.

thoughtProcess.title: 6. Intervals + 'how many concurrent' -> min-heap on end time.
thoughtProcess.body: Sort by start. For each interval, poll every heap root whose end time is <= the current start (those are finished), then push the current end. Heap size is the live count; its maximum is the answer. This is the meeting-rooms skeleton.

thoughtProcess.title: 7. Greedy needs a proof, not a hunch.
thoughtProcess.body: Before coding, argue it with an exchange: take any optimal solution, swap in your greedy first move, and show the result is no worse. If that argument does not go through, greedy is wrong and you are probably looking at a DP. Most wrong-answer greedy submissions are ones nobody tried to justify.

thoughtProcess.title: 8. Maximise non-overlapping intervals -> sort by END time.
thoughtProcess.body: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for everything after it. This is the opposite of the meeting-rooms count, which sorts by START and uses a heap on end times. Same input shape, two different sorts -- read which question is being asked.

thoughtProcess.title: 9. Pairing two sets optimally -> sort both, pair in order.
thoughtProcess.body: For minimising the largest gap or the total distance between two sets (mice to holes), sorting both and matching i-th to i-th is optimal. The exchange argument: any crossing pair can be uncrossed without making the result worse.

thoughtProcess.title: 10. 'Minimise total distance to a point' -> the median, not the mean.
thoughtProcess.body: Sum of absolute deviations is minimised at the median; sum of SQUARED deviations is minimised at the mean. Seats-style problems want the median. For an even count any point between the two middle values works, so take either.

keyPatterns.name: Min-heap greedy (always consume the two smallest)
keyPatterns.when: Cost of combining = sum of the two parts, and you must combine everything into one.

keyPatterns.name: K-th largest via size-K min-heap
keyPatterns.when: K-th largest / top-K, streaming or one-shot, K much smaller than N.
examples: A-th Largest Element in a Running Stream

keyPatterns.name: Two heaps for a running median
keyPatterns.when: Median after every insertion on a stream.

keyPatterns.name: Merge K sorted lists
keyPatterns.when: K already-sorted sequences into one sorted output.

keyPatterns.name: Interval overlap count (min-heap on end time)
keyPatterns.when: Minimum rooms / machines / platforms for overlapping intervals.

keyPatterns.name: Manual heapify / sift-down
keyPatterns.when: You must implement the heap yourself (no PriorityQueue allowed).

keyPatterns.name: Custom comparator on a value object
keyPatterns.when: You are ordering by a field (profit, expiry, end time) rather than a raw int.

keyPatterns.name: Activity selection (sort by end time)
keyPatterns.when: Maximise how many intervals you can finish without overlap.

keyPatterns.name: Sort both sides and pair in order
keyPatterns.when: Match two sets so the largest (or total) difference is minimised.

keyPatterns.name: Median minimises total absolute distance
keyPatterns.when: Gather everything to one position at minimum total cost.

keyPatterns.name: Two-pass greedy (satisfy each side independently)
keyPatterns.when: A constraint looks both left and right; one pass cannot see both.

commonMistakes.title: Max-heap for K-th largest
commonMistakes.wrong:
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
// then poll K times
commonMistakes.why: A max-heap of all N costs O(N) space and O(N + K log N) time. A min-heap capped at K is O(K) space and O(N log K), and it works on a stream where you never hold all N.

commonMistakes.title: Comparator written as a subtraction that overflows
commonMistakes.why: a - b wraps around when the difference exceeds int range, so the comparator returns the wrong sign and the heap silently orders incorrectly. Long.compare / Integer.compare are always safe.

commonMistakes.title: Rebalancing the two median heaps by guessing the side
commonMistakes.why: Guessing the side needs a non-empty check and still leaves the sizes unbalanced. Always push into one heap, move its root across, then correct the sizes -- it is branch-free and correct on the first element.

commonMistakes.title: Building a heap by N inserts
commonMistakes.wrong: for (int x : A) { heap.add(x); }   // O(N log N)
commonMistakes.right: for (int i = n / 2 - 1; i >= 0; i--) { siftDown(heap, n, i); }   // O(N)
commonMistakes.why: Bottom-up heapify is O(N) because most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a step or two. N inserts is O(N log N). Matters when N is 1e5 and you build repeatedly.

commonMistakes.title: Sorting intervals by end time for the meeting-rooms count
commonMistakes.why: Counting concurrent intervals requires processing in START order so that 'has this one begun yet' is meaningful. End-time sorting is for the different problem of maximising the number of non-overlapping intervals.

commonMistakes.title: Comparing the heap root with < instead of <= when releasing intervals
commonMistakes.why: A meeting that ends exactly when the next begins does not need a second room. Whether <= or < is right depends on whether intervals are half-open -- read the constraints and decide deliberately rather than by habit.

commonMistakes.title: peek() on an empty heap
commonMistakes.wrong: int top = pq.peek();   // NPE when unboxing null
commonMistakes.why: PriorityQueue.peek() returns null rather than throwing, so the crash surfaces later as an NullPointerException during unboxing -- far from the real bug.

edgeCases: Single element: connect-ropes cost is 0 (nothing to merge); the while loop must be size() > 1, not size() > 0.
K larger than N for K-th largest -- the answer is undefined; check and return -1 per the problem statement.
Running median on the very first element: upper is empty, so the rebalance must not peek it.
All values equal -- a comparator that returns a constant is fine, but do not assume any particular tie order.
Sums of merged ropes can exceed int when N is 1e5 and A[i] is 1e3; use long for the running total if constraints allow.
Merge-K-lists where some input lists are null or empty -- skip them before the first push.
Intervals that touch exactly (end == next start): decide <= vs < from the statement.
Empty input array: return 0 / -1 before touching the heap.
Duplicate values in a size-K heap are legitimate and must not be de-duplicated.
PriorityQueue iteration order is NOT sorted -- only poll() gives sorted order; never iterate the heap expecting order.
